It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional ray-casting volumetric rendering by leveraging standard graphics hardware polygon processing, offering real-time capabilities for complex repetitive scenes [S1].

The claim states that the method solves performance bottlenecks of traditional ray-casting by leveraging standard graphics hardware polygon processing to offer real-time capabilities for complex repetitive scenes. The evidence supports this in multiple ways: 1) The Abstract explicitly states the model allows for 'realistic of repetitive complex scenes' with 'lower cost of calculation due to the effective exploitation of the capacities of the graphics boards' and mentions 'Real time' in keywords. 2) The Introduction contrasts the method with traditional ray casting, noting that ray casting takes 5-20 minutes, whereas the new method exploits 'graphics boards treating, effectively, the polygons' to achieve real-time performance. 3) The text explicitly states 'The projection of a layer is faster than calculating projection for each voxel along a ray, providing an appreciable time benefit.' All specific facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

It differs from its parent [Voxel Coloring](4418-voxel-coloring.md) by shifting from a voxel-based storage model to a layered 2D texture model, and from siblings like [Generalized Voxel Coloring](5526-generalized-voxel-coloring.md) by explicitly utilizing 2D image layers for rendering rather than direct voxel traversal [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the method integrates 'voxel colouring' (referencing the parent technique) and converts the resulting volume into 'a set of layers (2D images considered as transparent textures)' (the layered 2D texture model). It further clarifies that this representation can be seen as a volume of voxels but is rendered by projecting and composing these 2D image layers using a Z-buffer, rather than performing direct voxel traversal or ray casting per voxel, which aligns with the claim's description of shifting from voxel-based storage/traversal to a 2D texture model for rendering.

This method renders volumetric textures by converting a reconstructed voxel volume into a set of 2D transparent image layers, which are then projected and alpha-composited onto the image plane using a Z-buffer [S1].

The claim states that the method renders volumetric textures by converting a reconstructed voxel volume into 2D transparent image layers, which are then projected and alpha-composited onto the image plane using a Z-buffer. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports every part of this claim: 1) It mentions converting the volume into 'a whole of layers (2D images considered as transparent textures)' (Abstract, Introduction). 2) It states these layers are 'projected and composed successively on surface defined as volumetric grid using the Zbuffer algorithm' (Abstract) and 'project and successively compose the layers on the image plan (ZBuffer)' (Introduction). 3) It details the alpha compositing process using the formula Cscreen = Alphapoint × Cpoint + (1 - Alphapoint) × Cscreen and mentions rendering transparent faces in depth order using the Z-buffer (Notes and Text). Therefore, all facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
